=== spec.md
# add-greeting: let alpha produce a greeting that beta prints

- size: project
- owner: demo-owner
- repos: [alpha, beta]
- supersedes: []
- approved: demo-owner 2026-10-01T09:00Z

## Why

Users of `beta` want a greeting on start-up, and the text belongs in `alpha`,
the shared library, so that other tools can use it too.

## Scope

In: the greeting text in `alpha`; printing it in `beta`.

Out: translations; any change to `gamma`.

## Requirements

### R1 Greeting text
`alpha` SHALL provide the greeting `hello, demo` for a caller that asks for it.

#### R1.S1 Default greeting
- GIVEN `alpha` at the branch head
- WHEN a caller asks for the greeting with no name
- THEN it gets the exact text `hello, demo` (11 characters, no trailing
  newline)

#### R1.S2 Name too long
- GIVEN a name of 65 characters
- WHEN a caller asks for the greeting with that name
- THEN it gets an error naming the 64-character limit, and no greeting

### R2 beta prints the greeting
`beta` SHALL print the greeting from `alpha` as its first line of output.

#### R2.S1 Start-up line
- GIVEN `beta` built against `alpha` at the branch head
- WHEN `beta` starts with no arguments
- THEN its first line of standard output is `hello, demo`, within 1 s of
  start (wall time)

## Approaches

1. Greeting in `alpha`, printed by `beta` (picked: one source of the text).
2. Greeting in `beta` only (rejected: other tools would copy the text).

## Open calls

1. The name limit is 64 characters, counted as Unicode code points.

# Plan: add-greeting

- change: add-greeting
- spec: changes/add-greeting/spec.md
- size: project

## 1. Goal and approach

`alpha` gains `greeting()`, which returns `hello, demo` and refuses a name
longer than 64 code points; `beta` prints that greeting as its first line of
output. Two build tasks, one per repo, with the project-level tests written in
parallel from the spec.

## 2. Interface contract

- alpha: `greeting(name: str | None = None) -> str`, in package `alpha`. With
  no name it returns `hello, demo`. With a name of at most 64 code points it
  returns `hello, <name>`. A longer name raises `ValueError`, whose message
  names the limit, 64.
- beta: `python3 -m beta`, with alpha importable, prints the greeting as its
  first line of standard output, then its existing banner `beta 1.0`.
- Project-level tests are Markdown files `test_R<n>_S<m>_<slug>.md` in
  `changes/add-greeting/tests/`, each with Given, When (one shell command, in
  which `$ALPHA` and `$BETA` are the alpha and beta checkouts of the commit
  set), Then and Fails if.
- Unit suites: `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` from the alpha root;
  `PYTHONPATH="$ALPHA" python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` from the beta
  root.

## 3. Global constraints

Verbatim from the spec:

- "it gets the exact text `hello, demo` (11 characters, no trailing
  newline)" (R1.S1)
- "within 1 s of start (wall time)" (R2.S1)
- "The name limit is 64 characters, counted as Unicode code points." (Open

---
name: mesh-post
description: Post one or more task/query messages into the agent mesh — addressed to a role (any holder claims it) or to a specific node's direct inbox — in one turnkey step. Writes schema-correct message files into the coordination repo, assigns globally-unique ids, and pushes. Use when you (as an operator, or as a node) want to ask a role to do something, fan one request out to several roles/nodes, or ping a node, in the hubless role-addressed mesh. Does not run the poller loop; it just drops messages.
allowed-tools: Read, Write, Bash, Glob, Grep
---

# mesh-post — turnkey SEND for the mesh

The mesh is peer-to-peer and role-addressed: no hub. To get work done you drop a
message into a **role queue** (`tasks/roles/<role>/`) and whichever node holds that
role claims it; or into a node's **direct inbox** (`tasks/<agent_id>/`) to ping or
pin work to one node. This skill sends such messages and pushes them. It is the
operator's SEND verb (`guidance/operator-interface.md`); a node may use it too. It
writes only the message file(s) it creates — never `status/**`, never anything else.

`mesh-post.sh` (next to this file) owns all the mechanics — identity, pull,
**globally-unique id assignment**, schema-correct frontmatter, queue placement,
scoped commit, and pull-rebase-retry push. Your only real job is the **body**:
expand the user's intent into a self-contained task the claiming node can run with
no history of this conversation.

## What you supply vs what the script does

You supply (judgment the script can't do):
- **body** — a markdown file with Goal / Context / Done when / On failure (for a
  `query`, Goal + Context is enough). Inline every path, commit, branch, prior
  result, and lore id the reader needs. This is the intelligence; write it well.
- **target(s), type, title** — and optionally priority, timeout, credentials,
  and the project memory space the task works in (`--project`).

The script does (every mechanical, error-prone part — do NOT do these by hand):
- resolves `from` (AGENT_ID from `~/.agent-identity.env`, else `<agent-id>`) and the
  repo path (REPO_PATH, else `--repo`);
- `git pull --rebase` first;
- assigns each message a **unique** id `<UTC-YYYYMMDDTHHMM>-<seq>`, where `<seq>`
  avoids every id already used this minute in any target queue, in `status/`, and
  earlier in the same run — so fanning one task out to N targets yields N distinct
  ids (status files are keyed by id in one global namespace, so shared ids collide);
- emits the §5 frontmatter (with `project:` as the line after `timeout_min:`
  when `--project` is given, and no `project:` line otherwise) and places each
  file in the right queue;
- **scope-commits only the files it wrote** (never `git add -A`), with a plain-text
  message, and pushes with up to 3 pull-rebase retries.

## Do this

1. Write the body to a temp file (e.g. `/tmp/mesh-post-body.md`). Make it
   self-contained; when fanning out to different OSes/nodes, write one body per
   variant and call the script once per variant.
2. Run the script:

```bash
<repo>/product/skills/mesh-post/mesh-post.sh \
  --to role:build --to role:geworker \
  --type task.request --title trilinos-spack-build \
  --priority normal --timeout-min 300 \
  --body-file /tmp/mesh-post-body.md
```

   Flags: `--to` (repeatable) is `role:<role>` or a bare `<agent_id>`; `--type` is
   `task.request` | `query` | `reply` | `task.cancel` | `library.submit` | …;
   `--title` is a kebab-case slug; optional `--priority low|normal|high` (default
   normal), `--timeout-min N` (default 120), `--credentials K1,K2` (KEY NAMES only,
   never values), `--depends-on id1,id2`, `--project proj:<name>`, `--from <id>`,
   `--repo <path>`. Add `--dry-run` to write + stage without commit/push when you
   want to inspect first.

3. Report to the user in one line per target: the target, the assigned id, and the
   file path — and that they will see the outcome (status/reply) on their next
   CHECK of the ledger. You do NOT wait here; the claiming node's poller senses the
   message on its next scan and routes any `reply` into your inbox
   (`tasks/<from-id>/`).

## Notes

- **`--project` loads a project space for the executor.** Give it when the task
  works in a project memory space: `--project proj:<name>`, matching
  `^proj:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$`. The claiming node loads that space for its
  executor (PROTOCOL §5, `spec/memory-spaces.md` §5). The script checks the
  value while it reads its arguments, before it looks at the repo, so an
  invalid value exits 1 with `mesh-post: invalid --project value: <value>` and
  writes no message. The space must be mounted on the bus (`spaces.yaml`);
  posting does not check that, and a claiming node that cannot find it blocks
  the task.
- **Type tells the consumer what it is.** `task.request`/`query`/`task.cancel` are
  claimable work (get a `status/<id>.json`); `library.submit` is drained by the
  librarian and gets no status; `reply` is information the recipient just surfaces.
- **Unstaffed role is fine.** Posting to a role no node currently holds just waits
  until one comes online. To check who holds a role:
  `grep -l "<role>" <repo>/agents/*.yaml`.
- **Git gate.** The script uses the literal `-C <repo>` form and a plain-text commit
  message, staging only its new files, so it stays inside the node git gate.
  Invoking mesh-post authorizes that one scoped commit+push — that is the skill's
  job; it does not touch the working tree's other changes.
mesh-post.sh

---
name: space-librarian
description: File records into a memory space (a Project Space or any other rw space) after the header-profile, reference and id checks, one commit per record, pushed to the space's main. Invoke when a librarian node files records into a space that spaces.yaml assigns to its role, when a session with no bus files a record into a space checkout, or when someone asks to file, check or desk-run records for a space.
allowed-tools: Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob
---

# space-librarian: file records into a memory space

A memory space (the memory-spaces design) is a git repo of records with one
writer per mesh, its librarian. This skill is that writer. It is given a space
root and record files, checks each record, and files the ones that pass: one
commit per record, pushed to the space's `main`. It needs no bus.

## Who runs it

- **On a mesh.** A mesh librarian uses this skill for every rw space that
  `spaces.yaml` assigns to its role: each entry with `access: rw` and its role
  in `librarian:`. It never writes a space listed `access: ro`. To list the
  spaces a role files (one-line entries, as the registry is written):

  ```sh
  grep -E 'access:[[:space:]]*rw' <bus root>/spaces.yaml |
    grep -E 'librarian:[[:space:]]*<role>[[:space:]]*[},]'
  ```

- **Without a bus** (single seat). The session uses this skill directly, on
  its checkout of the space, as its own librarian. The checks are the same;
  the real values they look for then come from the node alone.

It files what it is handed. Deciding what belongs in the space, and who may
hand it over, is the caller's job.

## Inputs

- **Space root**: the space's checkout, a git repo with `space.yaml` at its
  root and the space's remote as `origin`. In a bus it is `spaces/<path>`.
- **Records**: paths relative to the space root, each already written at that
  path. They are checked, and filed, in the order given.
- **Bus root** (optional). If not given, the bus is the space's superproject,
  else the `REPO_PATH` in `~/.agent-identity.env`. It counts only if it has
  `agents/`. With none, there is no bus.

## Output

One line per record, in the order given, and nothing else:

```
FILED <space path> <sha7>
REFUSED <space path>: <profile|reference|id> line <n>
```

`<n>` is the 1-based line of the record where the check failed. The checks run
in the order profile, reference, id, and the first that fails is reported, at
its first failing line. The output never holds the matched text or any value
the checks search for. A record path that names no file is an error for the
caller, not a result line.

## 1. Check each record

The three checks, as the check script `check.sh` runs them:

- **profile.** No real hostname, agent id, mesh task id or credential key
  name, and no home path, anywhere in the file. Real values come from the bus
  where one is present: `agents/*.yaml` (`agent_id`, `agent_name`,
  `hostname` and its first label, `credentials_available`, `cwd`), the
  direct-inbox names under `tasks/`, and the task ids in the file names under
  `tasks/`, `status/` and `_archive/`. From the node come the local hostname
  (`hostname` and `uname -n`, with their first labels) and the credential key
  names in `~/.agent-credentials.env`. Home paths are matched by four
  patterns:
  - the local `$HOME`;
  - each registered agent's `cwd`;
  - the first two path components of each registered agent's `cwd`;
  - absolute per-user paths under the macOS and Linux home roots.

  Generic `~/` paths are allowed, and so is an id-shaped example that no bus
  holds. Values shorter than three characters are skipped. Each value
  matches as a whole word. A hostname or credential key name inside a longer
  name joined by `-` or `_` passes. An agent id, agent name or task id joined
  that way does not, as in the bus's own `<task id>-<slug>` file names.
- **reference** (Markdown records). Every citation must resolve. A citation
  is a value of a front-matter reference field (`related`, `supersedes`,
  `superseded_by`, `discovered_in`), or a qualified cross-space id
  `<space id>/<record id>` in the body outside inline code and fenced blocks,
  where a space id is `core`, `lore`, `lore:<name>` or `proj:<name>`. A
  trailing `@<commit>` pin is ignored. It resolves when it is:
  - a URL;
  - a record id held by a record in the space (in its `id:` line, or as the
    start of its file name);
  - a qualified id whose space is listed in `may_reference` in `space.yaml`,
    or is this space (then the rest must resolve here);
  - a change id with a folder `changes/<id>/` or
    `changes/archive/<date>-<id>/`;
  - `<change>/T<n>`, where that change's `plan.md` has task `T<n>` as a
    heading or a table row.
- **id** (Markdown records). The id is the front-matter `id:`; under
  `decisions/` and `handoffs/` with no `id:` line it is the file name. A
  record with no id passes. An id already at this same path on `origin/main`
  (or `HEAD`, where there is no `origin/main`) is not new and passes. A new
  id must have the form
  `<category>-<YYYYMMDDTHHMMZ>-<4 hex>`, or the UTC-named form: `ev-<UTC>`,
  or `ev-<UTC>-<shard id>` for a shard (a task id and one lowercase letter),
  such as `ev-<UTC>-T19a`, under `changes/<id>/evidence/`; `<UTC>-<slug>`
  under `decisions/` and `handoffs/`. It must not be already present: no
  other file in the space holds it. Evidence, decisions and handoffs are one
  file per event, so a record there whose path is already on `origin/main`
  with other content is refused as `id`.

The script is `check.sh`, shipped beside this file in the skill's directory,
`<skill dir>`. Run that file with `sh` as it ships; never copy it into the
space or rebuild it by hand:

```
SPACE=<space root> sh <skill dir>/check.sh <space path> ...
```

Set `BUS=<bus root>` to name the bus. It prints `REFUSED ...` for a record
that fails, and `CHECKED <space path>` for one that passes. `CHECKED` is a
working line: those records go on to section 2, and it is never part of the
output. The script is POSIX `sh`, and its patterns are `grep -E`, `sed -E`
and POSIX `awk` (no `grep -P`, no GNU-only flag), so it runs unchanged with
BSD and GNU tools. The value lists it builds stay in its own temporary
directory, which it deletes on exit.

## 2. Commit, push, confirm

Take the `CHECKED` records one at a time, in order. Every git command names
the space root as a literal absolute path (`git -C <space root> ...`), never a
variable, so a git gate can see where it writes; where one is installed, its
allowlist must hold the space root. Messages are plain text on one line.

1. Fetch, and skip a record that is already filed:

   ```
   git -C <space root> fetch origin
   git -C <space root> cat-file -e origin/main:<space path>
   git -C <space root> diff --quiet origin/main -- <space path>
   ```

   If both of the last two exit 0, the record is on `origin/main` as it is.
   Make no commit; take as `<commit>` the output of
   `git -C <space root> log -1 --format=%H origin/main -- <space path>`, and
   go to step 5.
2. Commit the record alone:

   ```
   git -C <space root> add -- <space path>
   git -C <space root> commit -m "File <space path>" -- <space path>
   ```

   If git reports nothing to commit, an earlier run committed the record and
   stopped before its push; go on to step 3.
3. Bring the commit onto the tip, and find it:

   ```
   git -C <space root> fetch origin
   git -C <space root> rebase --autostash origin/main
   git -C <space root> log -1 --format=%H -- <space path>
   ```

   The last command prints `<commit>`. `--autostash` keeps records not yet
   filed out of the way of the rebase. Then run the check script again on
   this record alone, since the rebase may have brought in a record that now
   holds its id. If it prints `REFUSED`, undo the commit with
   `git -C <space root> reset -q HEAD~1`, print that line, and go on to the
   next record.
4. Push:

   ```
   git -C <space root> push origin HEAD:main
   ```

   If the push is rejected, repeat step 3 and push again, three pushes at
   most. If the rebase conflicts, run `git -C <space root> rebase --abort`.
   After a conflict, or a third rejected push, print nothing for this record
   or the ones after it, and tell the caller that filing stopped at this
   record.
5. Confirm with a fresh fetch:

   ```
   git -C <space root> fetch origin
   git -C <space root> merge-base --is-ancestor <commit> origin/main
   ```

   Only if it exits 0, print `FILED <space path> <sha7>`, where `<sha7>` is
   the first seven characters of `<commit>`.

## Desk run

When the caller asks for a desk run, run the check script (section 1) as
written, since it only reads. Then print each command of section 2 for each
`CHECKED` record, in order, with the space root, path and message filled in
and `<commit>` left as it is, and run none of them. A desk run prints no
`FILED` line.

## Never

- Print a matched line, a pattern list or a value from one, or write any of
  them inside the space.
- Commit more than one record in a commit, or commit a file it was not given.
- Force-push, push anything other than `HEAD:main`, or create a branch in the
  space.
- Write a space listed `access: ro`. This skill commits only in the space's
  own repo; it never commits to the bus or moves the space's gitlink there.
